full_judgment: 11. Generally when a Certificate is signed under section 6 of the PDR Act, a notice is served upon the certificate debtor under section 7 of the PDR Act and the certificate debtor is entitled to make a petition in the prescribed form signed and verified denying liability in whole or in part under section 9 of the Act within the period of 30 days from the service of any process for enforcing the certificate. Upon such denial of the liability under section 9 of the Act, the Certificate officer shall hear the petition, take evidence if necessary and determine whether the certificate debtor is liable for the whole or any part of the amount for which the certificate was signed and may vary, modify or set aside the certificate. So it is clear from these sections of the Public Demands Recovery Act that Certificate Officer has to determine whether the demand is due or not by sending notice of the demand to the certificate-debtor under section 7 upon which the certificate-debtor is entitled to put objection to the demand under section 9 and be heard under section 10 of the Act. These provisions ensure that no false or frivolous demand is made against the certificate debtor. The certificate issued under the PDR Act amounts to a decree which takes away or gives a valuable right. So ample provisions have been made in the PDR Act to safeguard the interest of the certificate-debtor; but by insertion of section 10A of the PDR Act by EP Ordinance XXV of 1961 certificate-debtor has been deprived of any opportunity of hearing to protect his right In the instant case it appears that there is sufficient dispute between the petitioner and the respondents as to the amount due. Had it been a case of admitted dues it should be a different case. Obviously the claim of the respondent Bank has not been admitted or determined by a statutory authority. We already found that a claim when admitted by borrower or fixed and determined in accordance with law becomes the dues recoverable under PDR Act, 1913, Recourse could not be had under PDR Act, 1913 to recover Bank's claim which has not been determined or admitted. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to section 5(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and contended that disputes of civil nature cannot be adjudicated by certificate officer, although sections 7, 9, 10 and 13 of the PDR Act, 1913 were intended to avoid injustice arising out of error or omissions. This section however did not contemplate adjudication of civil nature because certificate proceedings are initiated only for amount due, that is, amount already fixed and determined by authority prescribed by statute or by a competent Court. In support of his contention he cited the case of Miah Md. Latif Vs. Province of WP reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98, 100(10). We find there is much force in this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. He has further submitted that the insertion of section 10A, the provisions of sections 7, 9, 10 have been made inapplicable. Section 10A provides arbitrary power without provision for any hearing. So it is inconsistent with Article 31 of the Constitution and also with section 75 of the PDR Act, 1913.The learned counsel for the respondent could not refute this argument. Sections 7, and 10 are in consonance with natural justice also but they have been done away with by the insertion of section 10A of the PDR Act, 1913.
